implementation_notes: Scala's coroutine support is scala.concurrent.ExecutionContext plus libraries; the language itself has no suspend keyword. Scala provides continuations (scala.util.continuations) for the explicit, shift/reset control-effect, and Future composition for the practical case. Scala's macro-based frameworks (scala.concurrent's Future/Promise, Akka Streams, fs2) use a trampolined execution model where a Future's continuation is scheduled on an ExecutionContext - an implicit trampoline loop that avoids stack growth for chains. The idiomatic Scala answer to 'long sequence of async operations' is Future composition (flatMap/transform), which is a stackless continuation chain executed by the ExecutionContext's trampoline; a manual coroutine library is rare. Scala also has its own 'function colouring' avoidance via the ExecutionContext trampoline: a flatMap chain does not propagate any async marker because every step returns a Future.
idiom_name: Future/Promise chains executed by an ExecutionContext trampoline (shift/reset continuations for the explicit case)
pitfalls: Future chains do not cancel the underlying work when a downstream step fails - a timed-out Future may still be running the operation; use a cancellable source.
The default ExecutionContext.global is a shared fork-join pool; blocking inside it starves unrelated tasks - pass a dedicated dispatcher.
Implicit ExecutionContext is a hidden dependency that makes a Future's thread nondeterministic; supply it explicitly in library code.
scala.util.continuations (shift/reset) is powerful but low-level and rarely the right tool in application Scala - prefer Future composition.
